question: ‘The Crew 1’ was a game sold by the French video game developer Ubisoft until December 2023. However, it will become unplayable from April 2024, as the company will shut down the game’s servers1. 1.
Does this violate EU law?
In general, what limits does EU law impose on video game developers when decommissioning previously sold video games?
Which authorities are responsible for the enforcement of the rules?
answer: EU consumer protection legislation requires transparency about the material aspects of a trader’s offer, protects consumers against unfair commercial practices and contract terms, and provides consumers with remedies in the event of a lack of conformity. This legislation does not set specific requirements as to the duration of the supply of products, including of online video games.

Specifically, Directive 2019/770/EU (2) provides that, in the event of a lack of conformity, a consumer can require a supplier to bring the digital content/service into conformity or, where the supplier has made clear that it will not bring the content/service into conformity, to receive a proportionate reduction in the price or to terminate the contract.

In the event of termination of a contract for the supply of a digital service or content over a period of time, the provider must reimburse the consumer for the part of the price paid in advance for any remaining period of the contract affected by the termination. EU consumer legislation generally takes the form of directives which are transposed into the national laws of the Member States.

National courts and administrative authorities are competent to resolve individual cases and disputes. Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 (3) provides for a cooperation framework to allow national authorities of Member States to address cross-border breaches of consumer law in a coordinated manner.
